newsitem.title: UK: Futures market sees next UK govt upping rates soon.
newsitem.headline: Futures market sees next UK govt upping rates soon.

text.p: If the opposition Labour party clinches victory, as expected, in the British election on May 1, the first task facing the new Chancellor will be to raise interest rates soon, according to futures markets on Monday.
The June short sterling contract on LIFFE was down six basis points on the day at 93.51 by 1428 GMT, unchanged from before Prime Minister John Major confirmed May 1 as polling day.
This reflects market expectations that official interest rates will be somewhere around 6.25 or 6.50 percent by the end of June, up from their present 6.0 percent.

"The markets are assuming a Labour victory and that (shadow Chancellor) Gordon Brown will listen more intently to what the Bank of England has to say about long term inflationary pressures, and will put up interest rates," said Stephen Lewis, director of research at London Bond Broking.
"That's probably what will happen unless, over the next six weeks, we get a series of economic data that suggests inflation is less serious than the Bank thinks."
The opposition Labour party is widely tipped to trounce the Conservative government in the forthcoming election, with polls giving Labour around a 20 point lead over their age-old rivals.
Keen to shed a damaging image as a high spending, inflationary party, a new Labour government would act quickly on rates to establish market credibility, analysts said.

"Short sterling should pretty well have understood there will be a rate increase shortly after the election because the new Chancellor will want to establish credibility," said Tom Rayner, gilts analyst at Societe Generale.
Lewis agreed Brown would want to cultivate a hardline image.

"Brown would try to establish the credibility of both himself as a tough Chancellor and the Bank of England as an active player in monetary policy...in view of giving them more of a role down the line," he said.

He said the Labour party, which has taken a slightly more pro-European line than the Conservative government, would need to pay heed to the Bank of England if it wants to keep its European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) options well open.

"If Brown treats the Bank in a cavalier fashion like (Chancellor of the Exchequer) Kennth Clarke has done, the market will jump to the conclusion he has no serious intent regarding putting sterling into EMU," said Lewis.

Short sterling futures reflect expectations of where three-month British deposit rates will be at contract expiry. As three-month money tends to track base rates, short sterling is used as a yardstick for where the market sees base rates.
Lately, three-month money rates have been trading above base rates. As a result, it would take a fall to as low as 93.30 to reflect base rates of around 6.50 percent, analysts said.
David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy, said a lot of short sterling's movement in the coming weeks would depend on the currency.
"We should look at short sterling in the context of what is happening to the pound. Because we have fallen sharply today in terms of currency, short-sterling has fallen with it," he said.
"Not because there has been any big reassesment about prospects for interest rates, but because the exchange rate is viewed as the main factor preventing interest rates going up."
Coleman was more sanguine on the need to raise interest rates immediately after the election.

"As we have seen recently, some of the economic data have started to look a bit softer and if we do see a tighter fiscal stance from Labour then it is by no means guaranteed that they will need to put interest rates up as well," he said.
In such an uncertain environment, the big winner will be volatility, he added.
